'''''Iris japonica''''', [[common name|commonly]] known as '''fringed iris''', '''shaga''' and '''butterfly flower''', is a [[native plant|native]] of China and Japan. It is a [[species]] in the genus ''[[Iris (plant)|Iris]]'', in the subgenus ''[[Iris subg. Limniris|Limniris]]'' and within the ''Lophiris'' section. It is a [[rhizomatous]] [[perennial plant]], with pale blue, lavender or white flowers with an orange or yellow crest. It is cultivated as an ornamental plant in [[temperateness|temperate]] regions.

==Description==
''Iris japonica'' is similar in form to ''[[Iris confusa]]'', but the leaves are at ground level.<ref name=crested/>

It has short, slender, greenish, creeping rhizomes.<ref name=efloras/> It spreads by sending out thin, wiry,<ref name=crested/> long [[stolon]]s.<ref name=Lynch/> They are shallow rooted,<ref name=irisbotanique/> and form dense carpets and clumps.<ref name=american/> It is not [[invasive species|invasive]].<ref name=missouri/>

It has basal<ref name=efloras/> deep green,<ref name=Lynch/> dark green, yellowish green,<ref name=efloras/> or light green leaves.<ref name=india/> These are glossy (or shiny) on one side and dull on the other side.<ref name=crested/> They are tinted, reddish purple, close to the rhizome and do not have a midvein.<ref name=crested/> These lance-shaped leaves<ref name=sfgate/> can grow up to {{convert|25|-|60|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall and 1.5–3.5 cm wide.<ref name=efloras/> The leaves are generally described as [[evergreen]],<ref name=ClaireAustin/> and grow in a broad fan,<ref name=sfgate/> with arching tips.<ref name=missouri/>

It has wiry, stout stems that can grow up to {{convert|25|-|80|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall.<ref name=crested/> The 5–12 short, slender flower-bearing branches<ref name=american/> (or [[pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]s) are near the top of the plant.<ref name=efloras/> The stiff pedicels can reach between {{convert|1.5|and|2.5|cm|0|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=efloras/> The flowering stem (and branches) grow higher than the leaves.<ref name=Lynch/> The stems have 3–5 [[spathe]]s (leaves of the flower bud), which are lanceolate,<ref name=Lynch/> and {{convert|9.5|-|2.2|cm|0|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=american/>

The stems (and the many branches) hold between two and four flowers,<ref name=efloras/> in spring and early summer,<ref name=missouri/> between March and April (in Japan)<ref name=efloras/> or April and May.<ref name=handbook/>{{Verify source|date=May 2023|reason=There does not appear to be a mention for May in the source}}

The flowers are like ''[[Iris cristata]]'' flowers but paler and fancier. The short lasting flowers open in succession (one after another),<ref name=kew/> for between 2<ref name=handbook/> and 5 weeks.<ref name=ClaireAustin/> These flowers have a clove pinks aroma.

The flattish,<ref name=handbook/> flowers are {{convert|4.5|-|6|cm|0|abbr=on}} in diameter,<ref name=efloras/> and come in shades of pale blue,<ref name=crested/> or pale lavender,<ref name=handbook/> or lilac,<ref name=Lynch/> or purple,<ref name=kew/> to white.<ref name=crested/>

It has two pairs of petals, three large [[sepal]]s (outer petals), known as the 'falls' and three inner, smaller petals (or [[tepal]]s, known as the 'standards').<ref name=kew/> The falls are elliptic or obovate, with a spreading limb and blue or purple/violet blotching, spots, (or dots) around a central yellow signal patch around a visible yellow,<ref name=efloras/> or orange crest.<ref name=handbook/> They are {{convert|2.5|-|3|cm|0|abbr=on}} long and 1.4–2 cm wide. The standards are elliptic or narrowly obovate. They are {{convert|2.8|-|3|cm|0|abbr=on}} long and 1.5–2.1 cm wide. The standards spreading to the same plane as the falls,<ref name=alpine/> creating the 'flat' look. All the petals are fringed (fimbriated) around the edges.<ref name=efloras/>

It has a 1.1–2 cm long perianth tube, 0.8–1.2 cm long stamens, white anthers and 7–10 mm ovary. It has 0.5–0.75 long and pale blue style branches. The terminal lobes are fimbriated (fringed).<ref name=efloras/>

After the iris has flowered, between May and June, it produces an ellipsoid-cylindric, non-beaked seed capsule, which is 2.5–3 cm long and 1.2–1.5 cm wide. Inside the capsule, it has dark brown seeds with a small aril.<ref name=efloras/>

===Biochemistry===
Tetra-hydroxy-6-methoxyisoflavone, also known as Irilin D (C<sub>17</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O<sub>7</sub>), was found in ''Iris japonica'', ''Belamcanda chinensis'' (Iris domestica) and ''[[Iris bungei]]''. Junipergenin B (Dalospinosin) can be found in the leaves of ''[[Juniperus seravschanica]]'' and the roots of ''Iris japonica''.<ref>John Buckingham and V. Ranjit N. Munasinghe {{Google books|jFW3BgAAQBAJ|Dictionary of Flavonoids with CD-ROM|page=639}}</ref>

===Genetics===
As most irises are [[diploid]], having two sets of [[chromosome]]s, this can be used to identify hybrids and classification of groupings.<ref name=ClaireAustin/> Chromosome numbers in irises have been the subject of numerous studies. Findings include 2n=54, Kazuao, 1929; 2n=34,36, Simonet, 1932; 2n=36, Sharma & Tal., 1960; 2n=36 Kurosawa, 1971; 2n=31,33,54, Chimphamba, 1973; 2n=54, Mao & Xue, 1986; 2n=28,34,36,54, Colasante & Sauer, 1993; 2n=28, Dong et al. 1994; 2n=28 to 60 and Yen, Yang, & Waddick, 1995.<ref name=american/>

It is a [[triploid]] plant (3n chromosomes) that does not produce seed and therefore can not be propagated by vegetative means (seed or division) while in China, it can also be diploid. This is the reason why the Japanese think that a triploid specimen was imported from China to Japan. Then over time, it has become [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]]. Plants growing wild in Japan were counted as 2n=54 for infertile triploid forms. In China, wild forms are counted as 2n=36.<ref name=signa/>

==Taxonomy==
[[File:Iris-japonica.jpg|thumb|''Iris japonica'' illustration in ''[[Curtis's Botanical Magazine]]'', 1797]]
It has the common names of 'fringed iris',<ref name=kew/> 'Shaga' (in Japan),<ref name=biglobe/> and ''butterfly flower'' (in China).<ref name=tropical/>

It is written as {{lang|zh|蝴蝶花}} in [[Chinese characters|Chinese script]],<ref name=efloras/> and known as ''hu die hua'' in [[Pidgin]] in China.<ref name=efloras/> It is written as シ ャ ガ, 射干 in [[Japanese characters|Japanese script]].

The Latin [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''japonica'' refers to from Japan, even though the plant is thought to have originated in China.

''Iris japonica'' was first named by [[Carl Peter Thunberg]], (the Swedish botanist) in his 1784 publication, 'Flora Japonica'.<ref name=tropical/> It was introduced to Europe in 1792 from China, by Thomas Evans of the [[East India Company]].<ref name=kew/> It was then first published and described by Thunberg in ''Transactions of the Linnean Society of London'' (Trans. Linn. Soc. London) Volume 2 page 327 on 1 May 1794.<ref name=efloras/><ref name=american/><ref name=kew/> The species description was published in Curtis Botanical Magazine in 1797.<ref name=Lynch/> ''Iris fimbriata'' was later classified as a synonym of ''Iris japonica''.<ref name=plantlist/>

It has received an [[Award of Garden Merit]] from the [[Royal Horticultural Society|RHS]].<ref name=kew/><ref name=rhs/>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Iris japonica1.jpg|thumb|''Iris japonica'' growing in [[Osaka]], Japan]]
It is [[native plant|native]] to temperate and tropical regions of Asia.<ref name=grin/>

As it is a [[triploid]] plant in Japan, which means the plant does not produce any seed, all of the habitat expansion is thought to be artificial. Though it can be found in woods across Japan that appear wild, the plant's existence often indicates that the area used to be inhabited by humans and was abandoned.<ref>{{Cite book|last=岩槻|first=秀明|title=街でよく見かける雑草や野草がよーくわかる本|publisher=秀和システム|year=2006|isbn=4-7980-1485-0|location=|pages=}}</ref>

===Range===
It is found in China, within the [[Provinces of China|Chinese provinces]], of [[Anhui]], [[Fujian]], [[Gansu]], [[Guangdong]], [[Guangxi]], [[Guizhou]], [[Hainan]], [[Hubei]], [[Hunan]], [[Jiangsu]], [[Jiangxi]], [[Qinghai]], [[Shaanxi]], [[Shanxi]], [[Sichuan]],<ref name=irisbotanique/> [[Tibet Autonomous Region|Tibet]], [[Yunnan]], and [[Zhejiang]].<ref name=efloras/><ref name=grin/>

It is found in Japan on the islands of [[Honshu]], [[Shikoku]], and [[Kyushu]].<ref name=biglobe/>

In tropical Asia, it occurs in [[Myanmar]] (Burma).<ref name=kew/> In 2014, it was found in [[Mongolia]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Urgamal |first=M. |date=2014 |title=Additions to the vascular flora of Mongolia-II. |url=https://www.academia.edu/8843498 |journal=Proc. Inst. Bot. |publisher=Mongolian Academy of Sciences |volume=26 |pages=53–72 |access-date=15 August 2015}}</ref>

===Habitat===
''I. japonica'' grows on forest margins,<ref name=efloras/> in wet grasslands (or meadows),<ref name=efloras/> among rocks by streams,<ref name=kew/> and along hillsides,<ref name=sfgate/> or rocky slopes.<ref name=kew/> 
The species occurs at altitudes of {{convert|500|to|800|m|ft|abbr=on}} above sea level in Japan,<ref name=noah/> and {{convert|2400|to|3400|m|ft|abbr=on}} above sea level in China.<ref name=efloras/>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Iris japonica 5.JPG|thumb|''Iris japonica'' growing in [[Fukushima, Fukushima|Fukushima]], Japan]]
''Iris japonica'' is commonly cultivated in the USA.<ref name=crested/> It is the most commonly cultivated crested iris in the UK.<ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=stebbings/>

It is [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]] to between [[USDA]] Zone 7 and Zone 10.<ref name=missouri/> It is also hardy to European Zone H3.<ref name=European/> It is very easy to grow in a [[Mediterranean]] climate in sheltered positions.<ref name=missouri/>  Within the UK, it is hardy in [[Devon]] and [[Cornwall]],<ref name=Lynch/> and some other parts of southern UK.<ref name=handbook/> It prefers the protection of a sheltered sunny wall. Some cultivars of ''Iris japonica'' are more hardy than others.<ref name=handbook/> However, an extremely cold winter (or late frosts) may adversely affect the flowering of this species,<ref name=kew/> and the foliage becomes tatty,<ref name=stebbings/> or browned.<ref name=handbook/>

It should be grown in well-drained soils,<ref name=crested/> but moist soils are preferred.<ref name=sfgate/>  It can tolerate neutral or acidic soils (PH levels between  6.5 and 7.8).,<ref name=daves>{{cite web |title=PlantFiles: Orchid Iris, Crested Iris |url=http://davesgarden.com/guides/pf/go/33043/#b |publisher=davesgarden.com |access-date=30 March 2015}}</ref> though prefers slightly acidic soils (including peat banks).<ref name=stebbings/> It is not tolerant of salty water.<ref name=crestedau/>  It has average water needs during the growing season,<ref name=missouri/> wet or damp conditions during the winter may cause the root to rot.<ref name=missouri/> It can tolerate positions between full sun and partial shade,<ref name=crested/> but prefers partial shade.<ref name=missouri/>

It can be grown in a mixed [[Herbaceous border|flower border]], as a ground cover plant<ref name=missouri/> and can be also grown in containers in sheltered positions.<ref name=sfgate/>  The stems and dead leaves should be removed after flowering to keep the plant tidy and help it, for next years growth.<ref name=sfgate/>

In frost prone areas, it can be grown in a cool greenhouse.<ref name=Lynch/> The plants are rested in summer (after the spring flowering), and then started again in the late autumn. If it cannot be grown in a cool house, it should be given a sheltered position, with shrubs where it is protected from the morning sun.<ref name=handbook/>

It does not have any serious disease or insect problems,<ref name=missouri/> but pests (such as [[thrips]], slugs and snails), occasionally damage plants by feeding on the flowers or foliage.<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=sfgate/> The [[aphid]] ''[[Aulacorthum magnoliae]]'' can be found on the plant.<ref>R. L. Blackman, Victor F. Eastop {{Google books|UZqkLr9m4GUC|Aphids on the World's Herbaceous Plants and Shrubs|page=553}}</ref> It can be susceptible to attack by [[Japanese beetle]].<ref name=bulletin/>

===Propagation===
It can be propagated by [[Division (horticulture)|division]] or by seed growing.<ref name=sfgate/><ref name=daves/>
The seed is best sown in a cold frame, as soon as the capsules are ripe. Stored seed can also be sown in a cold frame in the Spring. Seedlings should be pricked out into small pots when large enough. They are then grown for another year in a greenhouse or cold frame. The new plants then can be planted into the ground in late spring or early summer of the third year.<ref name=daves/>
Division is best carried out after flowering during July or August. Large clumps of plants can then be re-planted in new sites. Smaller clumps should be potted and grown in a cold frame until there have formed sufficient roots to survive, they then can be planted in the Spring.<ref name=daves/>

==Toxicity==
Like many other irises, most parts of the plant are poisonous (rhizome and leaves), if mistakenly ingested can cause stomach pains and vomiting. Also handling the plant may cause a skin irritation or an allergic reaction.<ref name=kew/><ref name=daves/>

==Uses==
In Japan, it is used as a source of [[starch]]. The rhizomes are ground up to access the starch. In China, it is used in [[herbal medicine]]s, the rhizome is used to treat injuries. As a [[decoction]], it is used to treat [[bronchitis]], internal injuries, [[rheumatism]], and swellings.<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=kew/>

In Japan, the iris was encouraged or planted on the tops of hills, within [[castle]]s, the slippery fans of the iris leaves were used to slow marauding invaders to allow defending armies to protect the castle.<ref name=stebbings/>
